item.text: {"text":"Stronger negative competition is a plausible hypothesis, but weak margins alone do not establish the cause of Electronics performance. [gSASRec’s 2024 extended abstract](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2024/0939.pdf) supports replacing single-negative BCE with multiple negatives plus generalized BCE: recommended starting points are 128–256 negatives and calibration parameter t=0.75. This addresses sampling-induced overconfidence; it does not identify false negatives. [RecSys 2025’s corrected logQ work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09331) offers another practical direction: sampled softmax with uniform, in-batch, or mixed negatives, correcting sampling bias while accounting for the positive being deterministically present. Sampling-distribution correction and false-negative correction solve different problems.\n\nHard mining needs safeguards. [Hard-BPR (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19276) modifies the ranking loss to reduce false-negative influence under dynamic hard sampling. [R²NS (WWW 2026)](https://renzhaochun.github.io/assets/pdf/WWW_2026_Camera_Ready.pdf) documents early training failures from aggressive mining and motivates uniform warm-up followed by stochastic selection among high-scoring candidates, rather than always choosing the maximum. For this benchmark, a practical ablation is single-negative BCE versus multi-negative gBCE versus sampled softmax, then add warm-up and a modest hard-negative mixture to the strongest objective. Exclude padding, target collisions, and known training positives; unobserved positives remain uncertain. These are proposed experiments, not demonstrated gains on the four categories. Select using fixed macro validation HR@10 across all four datasets, report Electronics separately, and track GPU cost; diagnostic separation should remain supporting evidence."}
